Radar cross section (RCS) reduction is critical for stealth technology and can be achieved by coating microwave absorbing materials on target surfaces.
The study uses two composite materials with 10% and 35% carbonyl iron powders (CIPs) for matching and absorbing layers respectively.
Transmission line theory (TLT) is employed to model multilayer absorbers as cascaded transmission lines to calculate reflection coefficients.
Particle swarm optimization (PSO) is used to optimize layer thicknesses and number of layers to minimize reflection and maximize bandwidth.
Seven multilayer designs (Type I to Type VII) were developed with varying layer numbers and thicknesses.
Single-layer absorbers (Type I and II) showed narrow bandwidth and poor absorption performance.
The two-layer Type IV design achieved a bandwidth of 14.63 GHz from 3.37 to 18.0 GHz with a total thickness of 3.0 mm.
The five-layer Type VII design covers 2.0 to 18.0 GHz with a total thickness of 5.37 mm and improved low-frequency absorption.
Both Type IV and Type VII designs are insensitive to incident wave angles from 0° to 45° and to polarization changes.
Coating a PEC cylinder with Type IV or Type VII absorbers reduces monostatic RCS by at least 8 dB across most of 2.0–18.0 GHz.
Type IV coating provides up to 17.5 dB RCS reduction at 17 GHz; Type VII coating provides up to 16.5 dB at 12 GHz.
The reflection coefficient of the absorbers is used as a performance metric, with values below −10 dB indicating good absorption.
The matching layer (S1) has stable, low complex permittivity and permeability, aiding impedance matching.
The absorbing layer (S2) has higher complex permittivity and permeability, providing strong electromagnetic energy absorption.
Adding air gaps between layers (Type V, VI, VII) can improve absorber performance and bandwidth.
The designed absorbers maintain good absorption performance even on curved surfaces like cylinders.
The total thickness of the absorbers remains small enough for practical stealth coating applications.
The method combining TLT and PSO reduces design time and computational cost compared to full-wave EM simulations.
The absorbers cover the major radar frequency range from 2.0 to 18.0 GHz, which is important for military radar stealth.
The study demonstrates the feasibility of multilayer composite absorbers for broadband, angle-insensitive RCS reduction.
